multiple-choice.stem: Which sequence correctly follows food through the alimentary canal?
multiple-choice.correct: Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine
before: Mouth, trachea, stomach, pancreas, colon
Mouth, esophagus, liver, stomach, large intestine
Mouth, pharynx, gallbladder, jejunum, stomach
after: Mouth, pharynx, stomach, esophagus, small intestine, large intestine
Mouth, esophagus, stomach, large intestine, small intestine, anus
Mouth, pharynx, esophagus, stomach, ileum, duodenum, colon

multiple-choice.stem: How do mass movements differ from ordinary small-intestinal segmentation?
multiple-choice.correct: They move colonic contents long distances toward the rectum
before: They mechanically break down food in the mouth
They are caused by ciliary beating in villi
They are identical to bile emulsification
after: They repeatedly mix small-intestinal chyme in place without net propulsion
They are local mixing contractions of colonic haustra rather than long-range movement
They primarily move material from jejunum to ileum in short alternating segments

multiple-choice.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes visceral from parietal peritoneum?
multiple-choice.correct: Visceral covers organs; parietal lines the body wall
before: Visceral lines body wall; parietal covers organs
Both are layers beneath the muscularis externa in mucosa
Visceral surrounds only colon; parietal surrounds only stomach
after: Visceral lines the body wall; parietal covers organs
Both line the abdominal body wall and neither covers an organ surface
Visceral peritoneum lines the diaphragm only; parietal peritoneum covers the stomach

multiple-choice.stem: What connects the tooth root to the surrounding alveolar bone?
multiple-choice.correct: Periodontal ligament
before: Lingual frenulum
Greater omentum
Pyloric sphincter
after: The enamel covering the root
The gingival epithelium that lines the tooth neck
Cementum alone, without any connective-tissue attachment

multiple-choice.stem: Through which root-tip opening do vessels and nerves enter a tooth?
multiple-choice.correct: Apical foramen
before: Fauces
Esophageal hiatus
Major duodenal papilla
after: Pulp chamber
Root canal
Gingival sulcus

multiple-choice.stem: What is a major protective event during the pharyngeal phase?
multiple-choice.correct: The larynx elevates and the airway closes
before: The lower esophageal sphincter relaxes to prevent aspiration
The tongue initiates voluntary mastication
The pyloric sphincter contracts to protect the airway
after: The soft palate closes the nasopharynx while the laryngeal inlet remains open
The true vocal folds abduct widely to allow the bolus to pass
The upper esophageal sphincter stays tightly contracted as the bolus enters

multiple-choice.stem: What is the main purpose of stomach rugae?
multiple-choice.correct: Allow the stomach lining to expand as it fills
before: Provide villi for absorbing most dietary fats
Carry bile from the gallbladder
Convert pepsin to pepsinogen
after: Provide villus-like folds for nutrient absorption in the stomach
Prevent the gastric wall from expanding during a meal
Act as a muscular valve at the pyloric outlet

multiple-choice.stem: Why does gastric acid not normally destroy the stomach epithelium?
multiple-choice.correct: A mucus-bicarbonate barrier and epithelial defenses limit acid injury
before: Intestinal villi absorb all acid immediately
The stomach epithelium is composed of enamel
Hydrochloric acid is harmless to all human cells
after: Bicarbonate neutralizes all acid throughout the stomach lumen
Pepsin remains completely inactive in the acidic stomach
The stomach lining relies on rapid absorption of acid into portal blood

multiple-choice.stem: Why can the thought or smell of food stimulate gastric secretion before a meal?
multiple-choice.correct: Cephalic-phase vagal signaling prepares the stomach
before: The bile duct directly senses airborne odors
Food has already entered the ileum
Colonic mass movements force acid production
after: A stomach stretch reflex is triggered before food reaches the stomach
Olfactory receptors release gastrin directly into the bloodstream
Duodenal CCK is released solely in response to the smell of food

multiple-choice.stem: Which reflex can promote movement from the terminal ileum toward the cecum when the stomach becomes active?
multiple-choice.correct: Gastroileal reflex
before: Corneal reflex
Baroreceptor reflex
Pupillary reflex
after: Gastrocolic reflex
Enterogastric reflex
Defecation reflex

multiple-choice.stem: What is the most appropriate immediate response to excess acid arriving in the duodenum?
multiple-choice.correct: Increase bicarbonate delivery while restraining gastric emptying
before: Increase gastric acid release without limit
Switch off pancreatic ductal secretion
Absorb all acid into lacteals
after: Increase gastrin release while reducing pancreatic bicarbonate secretion
Accelerate gastric emptying to deliver more acid to the duodenum
Increase pancreatic protease secretion while inhibiting ductal bicarbonate release

multiple-choice.stem: Which structural sequence goes from larger folds to smaller surface specializations?
multiple-choice.correct: Plicae circulares, villi, microvilli
before: Microvilli, plicae circulares, villi
Lacteals, serosa, pylorus
Haustra, taeniae coli, pylorus
after: Villi, plicae circulares, microvilli
Plicae circulares, microvilli, villi
Microvilli, villi, plicae circulares

multiple-choice.stem: What is a lacteal?
multiple-choice.correct: Lymphatic capillary within an intestinal villus
before: Endocrine cell in a gastric gland
Branch of the hepatic portal vein
Muscular sphincter at the pylorus
after: Blood capillary inside an intestinal villus
Lymphoid follicle within an intestinal Peyer patch
Venous channel that drains directly into the hepatic portal vein

multiple-choice.stem: What is the brush border?
multiple-choice.correct: Microvillus-rich surface of enterocytes bearing terminal digestive enzymes
before: Inner circular muscle of stomach
Bile-producing lumen in liver
Macroscopic bands on colon
after: Mucus-rich coating lying above the intestinal villi
Circular folds formed by the intestinal mucosa and submucosa
The capillary network running through the center of each villus

multiple-choice.stem: Why are many pancreatic proteases secreted as inactive precursors?
multiple-choice.correct: To limit self-digestion of pancreatic tissue
before: To activate only after reaching the stomach fundus
To permit direct uptake by intestinal lacteals
To make them function as bile salts
after: Delay their activation until they have entered the bloodstream
Keep protein digestion restricted to the acidic stomach
Prevent bicarbonate from reacting with pancreatic enzymes

multiple-choice.stem: What is the primary role of Kupffer cells?
multiple-choice.correct: Macrophage-based immune surveillance and particle removal
before: Secretion of gastric acid
Formation of dental enamel
Production of pancreatic amylase
after: Synthesis of bile acids by liver parenchymal cells
Storage and concentration of bile before a meal
Support and organization of hepatic plates and sinusoids

multiple-choice.stem: During gallbladder contraction, which route carries bile toward the intestine?
multiple-choice.correct: Cystic duct, common bile duct, duodenum
before: Pancreatic tail, hepatic portal vein, stomach
Common hepatic duct, esophagus, jejunum
Cystic duct, left hepatic duct, stomach
after: Gallbladder, common hepatic duct, cystic duct, duodenum
Gallbladder, cystic duct, common hepatic duct, stomach
Gallbladder, cystic duct, portal vein, duodenum

flashcards.beforeFront: Name the instructor's seven digestive functions.
flashcards.afterFront: Name the seven major digestive functions.
flashcards.beforeBack: Ingestion, mechanical processing, chemical digestion, secretion, absorption, compaction, defecation.
flashcards.afterBack: Ingestion, mechanical processing, chemical digestion, secretion, absorption, compaction, defecation.

flashcards.beforeFront: What is motility, and is it on this lecture's seven-function list?
flashcards.afterFront: How do motility and compaction differ?
flashcards.beforeBack: Mixing/propulsion of contents; no, the list names compaction instead.
flashcards.afterBack: Motility mixes or propels contents; compaction removes water and concentrates feces.

multiple-choice.stem: How does pulmonary ventilation differ from gas diffusion?
multiple-choice.correct: Ventilation moves air in bulk; diffusion moves individual gas molecules down partial-pressure gradients
before: Ventilation is diffusion in alveoli; gas diffusion is movement of the diaphragm
Ventilation is movement of blood through lung capillaries; diffusion is movement of air in the trachea
Ventilation and diffusion both require ATP-driven pumps through the respiratory membrane
after: Ventilation and diffusion are both bulk flows driven by the same alveolar pressure gradient
Ventilation transports O₂ only; diffusion transports CO₂ only
Ventilation occurs across capillary walls, while diffusion occurs in the trachea

multiple-choice.stem: Why do nasal conchae help condition inspired air?
multiple-choice.correct: They increase mucosal contact and airflow mixing
before: They make the alveolar diffusion membrane much thinner
They change the diameter of the glottis during inspiration
They provide skeletal muscle contraction to drive the incoming airflow
after: They reduce the nasal mucosal surface exposed to moving air
They create a direct, unfiltered channel from the nostrils to the trachea
They serve as moving respiratory muscles that generate the inspiratory pressure gradient

multiple-choice.stem: Which observation is a defensible benefit of nasal compared with mouth breathing?
multiple-choice.correct: Incoming air is warmed, humidified, and filtered by the nasal passages
before: It bypasses the conducting airways so air reaches alveoli faster
It produces surfactant before air reaches the larynx
It removes all inhaled particles, unlike mouth breathing
after: They increase the amount of O₂ carried by each hemoglobin molecule beyond four
They perform the alveolar exchange of O₂ and CO₂ before air reaches the lungs
They prevent all contact between inhaled air and respiratory mucus

multiple-choice.stem: Why does the epithelial lining become very thin at the alveoli?
multiple-choice.correct: Minimize the diffusion distance for gas exchange
before: Withstand the mechanical abrasion of swallowed food
Provide more sites for cartilage attachment
Increase airway mucus storage capacity
after: Provide a thicker barrier against food abrasion
Maximize mucus production at the principal exchange surface
Provide room for cartilage to support individual alveoli

multiple-choice.stem: A person whose airway cilia are severely impaired would most directly struggle with what?
multiple-choice.correct: Removing mucus and trapped particles from conducting passages
before: Maintaining the affinity of hemoglobin for O₂
Keeping the alveolar basement membrane thin
Producing type II cell surfactant
after: Reduced O₂ affinity of hemoglobin without any airway secretions changing
Loss of type II pneumocyte surfactant synthesis without epithelial injury
Reduced ability of smooth muscle to dilate the bronchioles

multiple-choice.stem: How does increasing vocal-fold tension generally affect fundamental pitch, with other factors held constant?
multiple-choice.correct: It raises pitch
before: It lowers pitch in every circumstance
It eliminates the glottis
It changes only the loudness, never frequency
after: It lowers pitch by reducing the frequency of fold vibration
It changes only sound amplitude without affecting vibration frequency
It leaves the pitch unchanged if airflow continues

multiple-choice.stem: Why are tracheal cartilage rings C-shaped rather than fully circular?
multiple-choice.correct: They maintain patency while allowing the esophagus behind the trachea to expand
before: They allow the posterior tracheal wall to become a second gas-exchange membrane
They permit the trachea to fully collapse during every quiet expiration
They prevent the trachealis muscle from changing airway diameter
after: Their open side allows oxygen to diffuse through the tracheal wall
Their posterior gap permits the trachea to collapse fully during every breath
Their open side prevents posterior trachealis muscle contraction

multiple-choice.stem: Why do terminal bronchioles differ from respiratory bronchioles?
multiple-choice.correct: Terminal bronchioles conduct air without alveoli; respiratory bronchioles start bearing alveoli
before: Terminal bronchioles contain scattered alveoli, but respiratory bronchioles have none
Terminal bronchioles are supported by cartilage, but respiratory bronchioles are supported by bone
Respiratory bronchioles precede terminal bronchioles along the airway tree
after: Terminal bronchioles bear alveoli whereas respiratory bronchioles do not
Respiratory bronchioles contain cartilage rings while terminal bronchioles do not
Both types remain strictly conducting airways without alveoli

multiple-choice.stem: What crosses the lung hilum?
multiple-choice.correct: Bronchi, blood vessels, lymphatics, and nerves
before: Only pulmonary arteries but not veins or airways
Only the main bronchus, with no vessels or nerves
Alveolar ducts and individual alveoli from every lobule
after: Only the pulmonary artery enters; the bronchus and vein pass around the pleura
The bronchus and pulmonary vein pass through, but not lymphatics or nerves
Only alveolar ducts and individual exchange-capillaries enter the lung here

multiple-choice.stem: Why is pulmonary surfactant essential?
multiple-choice.correct: It reduces surface tension and limits alveolar collapse
before: It raises alveolar surface tension to generate expiration
It replaces hemoglobin as the primary O₂ carrier
It provides the ciliary drive for respiratory mucus clearance
after: It increases surface tension to make passive exhalation stronger
It primarily clears mucus from the trachea using ciliary movement
It forms the main thin cellular wall through which O₂ diffuses

multiple-choice.stem: What initiates normal inhalation?
multiple-choice.correct: Diaphragm and external intercostals contract, thoracic volume rises, alveolar pressure falls
before: Diaphragm relaxation raises thoracic volume and lowers lung pressure
Alveolar pressure rises above atmosphere before air is drawn inward
External intercostal contraction compresses the thorax to initiate inspiration
after: The diaphragm relaxes while thoracic volume increases and alveolar pressure falls
External intercostal contraction decreases thoracic volume to begin inspiration
Alveolar pressure rises above atmospheric pressure before air begins to enter

multiple-choice.stem: How does forced expiration differ from quiet expiration?
multiple-choice.correct: It actively recruits expiratory muscles such as abdominal muscles and internal intercostals
before: It remains driven entirely by passive recoil, only faster
It recruits only the diaphragm, which contracts downward during exhalation
It is generated solely by opening the glottis without changes in thoracic pressure
after: It depends chiefly on diaphragm contraction that increases thoracic volume
It occurs using passive recoil alone while expiratory muscles remain completely inactive
It lowers alveolar pressure below atmospheric pressure through abdominal contraction

multiple-choice.stem: What does Henry's law describe in respiratory physiology?
multiple-choice.correct: The dissolved concentration of a gas is proportional to its partial pressure and solubility at constant temperature
before: That dissolved gas concentration is independent of its partial pressure
That equal gas partial pressures imply equal dissolved concentrations for all gases
That gases enter blood by active transport rather than dissolution
after: The dissolved concentration depends on partial pressure but not gas solubility
Equal partial pressures cause identical dissolved concentrations for all gases
It describes bulk airflow caused by changes in chest volume

multiple-choice.stem: Why does CO₂ diffuse from pulmonary capillaries toward alveolar air?
multiple-choice.correct: Incoming blood PCO₂ exceeds alveolar PCO₂
before: Alveolar PCO₂ is greater than arriving pulmonary capillary PCO₂
CO₂ is actively pumped toward higher partial pressure in the alveolus
Hemoglobin carries CO₂ only as a dissolved gas and cannot release it in lungs
after: Alveolar PCO₂ is normally greater than PCO₂ in arriving venous blood
Oxygen binding to hemoglobin directly forces CO₂ into alveolar air regardless of gradients
CO₂ crosses the membrane only by active transport rather than diffusion

flashcards.beforeFront: List the seven respiratory functions emphasized in the lecture.
flashcards.afterFront: Name the seven major respiratory functions.
flashcards.beforeBack: Exchange gases; move air; condition and protect respiratory surfaces; defend against pathogens/pollutants; produce sound; support smell; regulate pH.
flashcards.afterBack: Gas exchange, air movement, environmental protection, defense, sound production, olfaction, acid–base regulation.

flashcards.beforeFront: State the lecture's simplified DRG/VRG functions, with a caution.
flashcards.afterFront: How do the DRG and VRG contribute to breathing?
flashcards.beforeBack: DRG emphasizes inspiratory/sensory integration; VRG is recruited for broader inspiratory/expiratory demands; in reality they are interacting networks.
flashcards.afterBack: DRG supports inspiratory integration; VRG includes neurons for rhythm and stronger inspiratory or expiratory activity.

multiple-choice.stem: What are the three principal functions of the lymphatic system emphasized in Chapter 22?
multiple-choice.correct: Return tissue fluid to blood, support immune defense, and transport absorbed intestinal fats
before: Make red cells, pump blood, and secrete bile
Produce digestive enzymes, store calcium, and release hormones
Carry oxygen to tissue, synthesize glucose, and excrete urea
after: Return fluid directly to arteries, initiate immunity, and deliver lipids mainly through portal blood
Produce antibodies in lymphatic vessels, recirculate red blood cells, and move dietary fat into bile
Return interstitial fluid to capillaries, carry all dietary nutrients through lymph, and eliminate immune surveillance

multiple-choice.stem: A patient develops swelling after lymph vessels are surgically damaged. Which mechanism best explains the swelling?
multiple-choice.correct: Interstitial fluid is not being returned to the blood efficiently
before: Capillary filtration has stopped completely
The spleen produces an excess of red blood cells
The kidneys no longer make antibodies
after: Capillary filtration into the damaged tissue has ceased completely
Local venous return increases enough to remove all extracellular fluid
Protein-rich fluid is cleared more rapidly despite the lymphatic obstruction

multiple-choice.stem: A fluid sample is taken from between muscle cells and then from an adjacent lymphatic vessel. What changes in its name?
multiple-choice.correct: It is called interstitial fluid in tissue and lymph inside the lymphatic vessel
before: It is called serum in tissue and bile in the vessel
It is plasma in tissue and cerebrospinal fluid in the vessel
It is always called whole blood regardless of location
after: The fluid is lymph in tissue spaces and becomes interstitial fluid after entering a vessel
The fluid is called plasma in tissue spaces and lymph inside a blood venule
The names are interchangeable regardless of where the fluid is located

multiple-choice.stem: Why is the lymphatic system important to maintaining blood volume?
multiple-choice.correct: It returns part of the fluid filtered out of blood capillaries to the venous circulation
before: It supplies most of the force that pushes blood through arteries
It prevents all fluid from leaving blood capillaries
It synthesizes plasma albumin in lymph nodes
after: It provides the pressure that pumps blood from the heart through arteries
It prevents any filtration of plasma water out of blood capillaries
It replaces the venous circulation as the main return path for whole blood

multiple-choice.stem: After a meal rich in long-chain triglycerides, which fluid may have a milky appearance?
multiple-choice.correct: Chyle in intestinal lymphatics
before: Cerebrospinal fluid
A typical arterial plasma sample before fat absorption
Urine in the renal pelvis
after: Venous plasma in the lower limb after ordinary fasting
Lymph draining the lungs before any intestinal lipid absorption
Interstitial fluid in muscles that does not contain absorbed lipoproteins

multiple-choice.stem: Which pressure generally promotes movement of water outward across blood capillaries?
multiple-choice.correct: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
before: Erythrocyte oxygen affinity
Intracellular nuclear pressure
Pressure generated by thymic T-cell development
after: Plasma oncotic pressure exerted by circulating albumin
Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure acting toward the capillary
A reduced capillary pressure relative to the surrounding interstitium

multiple-choice.stem: Which structural difference helps initial lymphatic capillaries take up interstitial fluid?
multiple-choice.correct: Their overlapping endothelial cells form pressure-sensitive entry flaps
before: They have a thicker continuous basement membrane than blood capillaries
They are sealed by valves that prevent inward fluid movement
They contain red blood cells that generate pressure
after: A thick, continuous basement membrane that prevents protein entry
Rigid endothelial tight junctions that never change with tissue pressure
A continuous muscular wall that generates high intraluminal suction

multiple-choice.stem: What happens when tissue pressure rises outside a lymphatic capillary?
multiple-choice.correct: Entry flaps can open to admit fluid and anchoring filaments can help prevent collapse
before: All initial capillaries seal permanently
Lymph is actively pumped outward into tissues
The thoracic duct closes its connection to veins
after: The flaps close more tightly so fluid is retained in the tissue
Fluid exits the lymphatic capillary directly through the open flaps
Only collecting-vessel valves change, while initial capillary entry remains unaffected

multiple-choice.stem: A person walks after sitting immobile for hours. Why might lymph return from the legs improve?
multiple-choice.correct: Muscle contractions compress collecting vessels and valves direct the fluid centrally
before: Arteries convert into lymphatic capillaries during exercise
The spleen begins pumping leg lymph directly
Lymphocytes create hydrostatic pressure by dividing
after: Skeletal muscle relaxation creates an equal pressure throughout every collecting vessel
Movement closes all valves simultaneously and stops lymph transport
Leg-muscle contraction forces lymph outward into surrounding tissues

multiple-choice.stem: How does breathing support lymph drainage?
multiple-choice.correct: Changes in thoracic and abdominal pressure help draw and propel lymph centrally
before: Every inhalation opens blood vessels directly into the pleural cavity
The diaphragm secretes chylomicrons during inspiration
Breathing prevents all liquid from entering initial lymphatics
after: Breathing increases abdominal pressure without changing thoracic pressure
Thoracic pressure changes reverse the one-way valves after each breath
Respiratory movements directly pump lymph out of venous blood back into tissues

multiple-choice.stem: Which statement about lymphatic pumping is most accurate?
multiple-choice.correct: Flow uses valves, body movement, breathing, and rhythmic collecting-vessel contraction without a single heart-like pump
before: Only the heartbeat moves lymph through lymphatic vessels
Lymph flow occurs solely by diffusion from foot to neck
Lymphatic capillaries generate blood pressure equal to the aorta
after: A central pump creates arterial-level pressure throughout collecting lymphatics
External movements alone propel lymph; collecting-vessel walls cannot contract
The flow relies on passive diffusion with no role for valves or pressure changes

multiple-choice.stem: A lymphatic tracer enters the LEFT foot. Which route is appropriate?
multiple-choice.correct: Left lumbar drainage toward cisterna chyli, thoracic duct, then left venous angle
before: Right jugular trunk directly into right venous angle
Right subclavian trunk into right lymphatic duct
Splenic artery into the lung
after: Left leg → left jugular trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
Left leg → right subclavian trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle
Left leg → left lumbar trunk → right lymphatic duct → right venous angle

multiple-choice.stem: What is the principal activity of a germinal center during a response?
multiple-choice.correct: Activated B-cell proliferation and affinity-related selection
before: Erythrocyte synthesis
Synthesis of digestive enzymes
Production of chylomicrons
after: Activated T cells mature into red-pulp macrophages inside follicles
Naïve B cells leave the node without proliferation or differentiation
T cells undergo thymic positive and negative selection inside the germinal center

multiple-choice.stem: What is the functional advantage of bringing antigen and lymphocytes into lymph nodes?
multiple-choice.correct: It facilitates antigen sampling and encounters among antigen-presenting cells and lymphocytes
before: It prevents any fluid from entering the bloodstream ever again
It forces all lymphocytes to become macrophages
It replaces the need for innate defenses
after: It ensures that every lymphocyte recognizes every antigen equally
It replaces the need for T-cell costimulation and innate signaling
It prevents all antigens from leaving the subcapsular sinus

multiple-choice.stem: How can circulating naive lymphocytes enter a lymph node without arriving in afferent lymph?
multiple-choice.correct: Through specialized high endothelial venules
before: By swimming upstream through the thoracic duct
By crossing from the common bile duct
Through red pulp sinusoids of the spleen
after: Through afferent lymphatics exclusively, never directly from blood
Through large arterial branches opening directly into the follicular cortex
Through efferent lymphatics by reverse flow into the paracortex

multiple-choice.stem: What is the central purpose of the blood–thymus barrier, particularly in the cortex?
multiple-choice.correct: Limit premature exposure of developing thymocytes to circulating antigens
before: Force all B cells into the thymus
Drain intestinal fats through the thymus
Keep mature memory T cells from entering blood permanently
after: Keep all circulating antigens permanently inside the thymus medulla
Prevent thymic epithelial cells from contacting immature thymocytes
Completely separate thymocytes from self-antigen presentation during selection

multiple-choice.stem: Why does thymic negative selection matter?
multiple-choice.correct: It helps remove or control developing T cells that strongly recognize self-antigens
before: It converts T cells into red blood cells
It trains B cells to secrete digestive enzymes
It removes every T cell that recognizes any self-MHC at all
after: Eliminate all thymocytes that recognize self-MHC at any strength
Guarantee that every mature T cell can react against all tissue antigens
Select cells only for the ability to secrete antibodies in the thymus

multiple-choice.stem: How does splenic immune surveillance differ fundamentally from lymph-node surveillance?
multiple-choice.correct: Spleen primarily filters blood, whereas lymph nodes primarily filter lymph
before: Spleen filters air while lymph nodes filter urine
Both filter only bile and never encounter antigens
Spleen filters lymph but lymph nodes filter blood exclusively
after: Spleen chiefly filters lymph; lymph nodes chiefly filter circulating blood
Both filter circulating blood equally, but only lymph nodes contain immune cells
Spleen and lymph nodes both receive antigen primarily through afferent lymphatic vessels

multiple-choice.stem: What enters and leaves the spleen at its hilum?
multiple-choice.correct: Splenic artery and vein
before: Afferent lymphatic vessels in large numbers
Pancreatic secretions and bile
Pulmonary artery and vein
after: Splenic artery and thoracic duct
Afferent and efferent lymphatics forming the node-like sinus system
Portal vein and hepatic artery

multiple-choice.stem: What happens to iron from many aged red blood cells removed by splenic macrophages?
multiple-choice.correct: It can be recovered and recycled for future hemoglobin synthesis
before: It is always excreted unchanged through bile within minutes
It becomes a lymphatic valve
It is destroyed along with the heme ring
after: It is all eliminated without reuse when hemoglobin is degraded
It is retained inside splenic macrophages and never enters circulation again
It is converted directly into bilirubin and cannot be used for new hemoglobin

multiple-choice.stem: Which consequence is clinically important after removal of the spleen?
multiple-choice.correct: Increased susceptibility to severe infections by some encapsulated bacteria
before: Complete loss of all T-cell production at every age
Permanent inability to absorb glucose
Inability to pump venous blood toward the heart
after: Loss of circulating lymphocytes because no T cells can mature outside the spleen
A complete loss of antigen-specific immune memory after splenectomy
Reduced defenses against encapsulated bacteria because all lymph nodes stop working

multiple-choice.stem: Why can trauma to the spleen be medically dangerous?
multiple-choice.correct: Its highly vascular tissue can bleed extensively into the abdomen
before: It contains digestive acid that dissolves abdominal organs
A splenic rupture blocks breathing by closing the trachea
It is the only organ producing all antibodies
after: The spleen lacks a connective-tissue capsule and therefore always ruptures
Its thin-walled sinusoids contain no blood until after a traumatic injury
A ruptured spleen primarily blocks lymph drainage without causing bleeding

flashcards.beforeFront: Why should the study-guide B-cell hormone question be flagged?
flashcards.afterFront: Where do B cells develop, and which cells mature in the thymus?
flashcards.beforeBack: The lecture identifies thymosin-related signals for T-cell maturation, not a single standard required hormone for B-cell differentiation. B-cell maturation normally occurs in bone marrow.
flashcards.afterBack: B cells develop primarily in bone marrow; T cells mature and undergo selection in the thymus.

flashcards.beforeFront: Describe the lecture's simplified route of splenic blood flow.
flashcards.afterFront: Trace the main route of blood through the spleen.
flashcards.beforeBack: Splenic artery → branching/trabecular and central arteries → red pulp/sinusoids → venous drainage → splenic vein.
flashcards.afterBack: Splenic artery → branching and central arteries → red pulp and sinusoids → splenic vein.
